title: EMDRIA: screen reader readability (Immersive Reader equivalent)
body:
**Status (initial assessment):** Gap: upstream work in progress

## Requirement
Content and navigation are usable with a screen reader, with readability comparable to Immersive Reader.

## What Frappe LMS offers
A community WCAG 2.1 AA audit of Frappe UI (the Vue component library underneath Frappe LMS), reported as May 2026, found and filed open issues. This is a current, significant risk to the requirement.

> Assessment below is from initial desk research against Frappe LMS docs and community threads; **not yet verified on our instance**. Part of this issue is confirming or correcting it.

## To do: human review and configuration
- [x] Find the upstream audit and its open issues in frappe/frappe-ui and frappe/lms; link them here and note which affect learner-facing pages (frappe-ui#639-#643, #1205, #1036; mapped in `docs/accessibility/README.md`)
- [ ] Run our own pass with NVDA (Windows) and VoiceOver (macOS/iOS) through: login → course list → lesson → quiz → assignment → certificate (checklist and findings template are in `docs/accessibility/`; not yet run)
- [x] Run an automated scan (axe / Lighthouse) on the same pages and record the results (axe, `docs/accessibility/axe-summary.md`; merged in #47)
- [x] Decide what we fix in our fork versus wait for upstream, and whether an "Immersive Reader"-style reading mode is needed or native browser readers are enough (decided: fix `lms` code only and leave frappe-ui upstream; native browser readers are enough, so no custom reading mode. Per-finding decisions follow the manual pass)

## Done when
A documented screen-reader walkthrough of the learner journey with no blocking issues, or a tracked list of remaining fixes with owners.

title: Accessibility: keyboard navigation and screen-reader pass
body:
Accessibility was an explicit commitment in the project report. #14 covers **audio narration only** — this is the keyboard and screen-reader half, and it is largely **verification rather than construction**.

Already built into the DOM dialogue overlay: `role="dialog"`, `aria-live`, focus management, and 1–9 key selection for choices. The work is confirming it behaves, not adding it.

- [ ] Walk a full dialogue exchange using **keyboard only** — no mouse
- [ ] Verify focus moves into the dialogue on open and returns sensibly on close
- [ ] Test with an actual screen reader (NVDA on Windows is free) and confirm dialogue text and choices are announced
- [ ] Confirm `aria-live` announces new dialogue nodes without the reader losing its place
- [ ] Check NPC markers are discoverable without relying on sight alone — coordinate with #15
- [ ] Note anything the pointer-lock navigation makes impossible, and write it up honestly as a known limitation rather than claiming coverage we do not have

The 3D navigation itself will not be fully accessible; say so in the report rather than overclaiming.

title: Testing: run manual screen-reader accessibility pass
body:
## Owner
Human accessibility testers.

## Goal
Run real assistive-technology checks before App Store submission. Existing accessibility-tree evidence is useful but is not a substitute for screen-reader testing.

## Suggested matrix
- NVDA + Firefox or Chrome on Windows.
- VoiceOver + Safari on macOS or iOS.
- Orca + Firefox on Linux, if available.

## Scope
Exercise at minimum:
- main navigation to Library;
- catalogue search/filter controls and result updates;
- mobile/filter panel if using a narrow viewport/device;
- item details drawer/page and editable metadata fields;
- metadata import preview/apply flow;
- settings root picker and scan controls;
- loading/error/status announcements where applicable.

## Acceptance criteria
- Tester reports identify tested AT/browser/OS combinations.
- Keyboard and screen-reader blockers are filed as separate bugs.
- No severe navigation, focus, naming, or destructive-action ambiguity remains untriaged before release.

## Verification
Reports include the exact app version/package and concise notes for pass/fail per surface.

title: Make the trainer usable with a screen reader
body:
Make the trainer genuinely usable with a screen reader. This is the part of
accessibility that automated tooling cannot check, so it needs its own issue and
manual testing.

Axe already runs against every view in both themes in CI. Axe cannot see any of
what follows.

### The problem this solves

A typing trainer is close to the worst case for a live region. Announcing every
keystroke produces a firehose that makes the app unusable; announcing nothing
leaves a screen reader user with no idea where they are.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Individual keystrokes are **not** announced.
- [ ] The current word is announced when it changes.
- [ ] Errors are announced.
- [ ] The end-of-drill result is announced once.
- [ ] Progress uses a polite live region; the result uses assertive. Not the
      reverse.
- [ ] The drill surface has an accessible name, and a description stating the next
      key, the finger and the row.
- [ ] Nothing about progress, error state or key state is conveyed by colour alone.
- [ ] `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` removes every transition and any
      celebratory animation.

### Manual testing required

Tested with at least VoiceOver on macOS and NVDA on Windows. The checklist in
`docs/accessibility.md` is the acceptance criteria; tick it off in the pull
request and say which assistive technology and version you used.

### Tests this unblocks

- End-to-end: *announces the current word and the result, but not every
  keystroke*. That test can only check the regions and their politeness, not
  whether the result is actually usable. The manual pass is the real test.

### Help wanted

If you use a screen reader and would be willing to try this, that feedback is
worth more than anything the tooling can tell us.

title: New shared skill: arabic-a11y (screen readers and accessible Arabic UI)
body:
[`arabic-ui`](https://github.com/asasemahmed/arabkit/blob/main/shared/skills/arabic-ui/SKILL.md) touches accessibility, but Arabic has specific problems that deserve their own skill.

## Proposed structure

Based on [@Kin230k's proposal](https://github.com/asasemahmed/arabkit/issues/14#issuecomment-5867124433) below.

### 1. `SKILL.md`: durable semantic rules

- Correct `lang` at the smallest meaningful language change, with page direction inherited.
- Code, URLs, emails, phone numbers, hashes, and identifiers kept as explicit LTR islands, without changing the direction of the surrounding sentence.
- Accessible names that agree with the visible Arabic labels.
- DOM and focus order that do not change merely because the layout is RTL.
- Status and error relationships (field errors, error summaries, live regions) that survive translation.

### 2. `references/`: versioned screen-reader observations

VoiceOver, TalkBack, and NVDA behavior depends on OS, browser, synthesizer voice, locale, and screen-reader version, so it lives in reference tables rather than in the rules. Each fixture records:

- the Arabic/English string, markup, and attributes;
- the expected accessible name, value, and state;
- the expected focus transition or announcement;
- the exact environment and date of the observed output.

### 3. First fixture matrix

- Arabic prose beginning with an English product name
- Arabic labels with email, URL, code, phone, or model-number values
- Arabic-Indic versus Western digits
- Optional diacritics
- Field errors and an error summary
- Async success and failure updates
- A modal returning focus after close

## Boundaries

`arabic-a11y` owns the semantic contract and real screen-reader verification. [`arabic-ui`](https://github.com/asasemahmed/arabkit/blob/main/shared/skills/arabic-ui/SKILL.md) owns visual design and [`arabic-rtl`](https://github.com/asasemahmed/arabkit/blob/main/shared/skills/arabic-rtl/SKILL.md) owns bidi implementation mechanics.

## Quality gate

No platform-specific observation is presented as universal unless it has been reproduced across the named environments.

Experience from people who use or test with Arabic screen readers is especially valuable here.

title: VoiceOver accessibility issues
body:
**Description**
Given all the issues I've reported so far have been accessibility ones I figured I might as well try VoiceOver (iOS's screen reader) and see how it was.

I can navigate around the UI fine, but:

* Every single button is reported as just "Button". This can probably be fixed with [`accessibilityLabel`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiaccessibilityelement/accessibilitylabel).
* Trying to activate boost or favourite buttons triggers no UI update until the UI is repainted (ie opening the post view or reopening the app) so it seems like boost/favourite do nothing.
* Trying to drag around the focus with single finger tap and drag begins scrolling extremely fast near the top or bottom edges. I suspect this is because it's focusing to the next major UI element, which is the next post. Native SwiftUI apps do not have this problem because they refuse scrolling when dragging around the focus.
* The entire UI becomes untouchable (action rejected sound) if I open any dropdown (timeline selector ie) and then try to navigate out (ie tap outside of the menu). Native UI elements say "Close context menu" when this is done instead. The return gesture (two finger scrub) does work to close the menu and return focus to the parent element so this isn't major.
* The tab selectors at the bottom straight up don't work. Trying to select the notification tab does absolutely nothing.
* Somehow the "post characters remaining" hint is read out as individual digits instead of as a full number (ie my instance's limit of 102,400 is read out as "one zero two four zero zero" instead of "one hundred two thousand four hundred")
* Navigating over emoji in the emoji picker requires moving to the next element twice to move one emoji. This is because the first object is read as "Button" which I imagine is "select this emoji", while the second object is slightly smaller than the first and reads the actual emoji name. I *believe* (not certain) this could be done by setting `accessibilityLabel` to "Insert emoji" and [`accessibilityValue`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiaccessibilityelement/accessibilityvalue) to the emoji name.
* Settings do not have their current state read out when hovered. Their child element (ie the boolean toggle) is selectable (this is not how it's done in the settings app and most other settings UIs) but also does not read out the current state. In other words there's no indication of the current state at all to a user without sight. Ideally this would be fixed by following other apps and making activating the label toggle the element and read state, instead of having a child checkbox element at all. This is probably doable with [`accessibilityTraits`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiaccessibilityelement/accessibilitytraits). This works fine with settings elements that are dropdowns (the default post visiblity).
* Focusing a photo without alt text just reads out "Button" instead of "Image".

I imagine most of these are upstream UI framework issues but I figured I would note these anyways. This is in my testing as a fully sighted user so I am absolutely certain I missed some.

If you need additional explanation or a video of any specific ones to understand let me know and I can do so.

**Environment**
 - Device: iPhone 15 Pro Max
 - OS: iOS 26.6
 - App version: 0.0.6-alpha (65b5010@master)

title: Dictation quality AX.1: The default Dictate shortcut, Control and Option held, is VoiceOver's own modifier pair, so a VoiceOver user's navigation starts and cancels recordings
body:
> **Implementation order 626 of 946. Wave 5: Context-read consumers and insertion hardening.**
> **Do first:** #3558

**Problem.** Scenario: a screen-reader user moves through a window with the VoiceOver keys held (Control and Option) and presses an arrow repeatedly. A new install dictates with exactly that pair held (`HotkeyBinding.controlOptionHold`, `Docs/shortcuts.md` "The dictation shortcut a new install gets"). `DictationController` settles a modifier-only press for 200 ms (`modifierSettle`) and then acts, so any VoiceOver chord held longer than that opens the microphone, plays the start cue and posts the "Listening." announcement (`DictationAnnouncement.swift:30`), and the next key withdraws the press and cancels the dictation. Nothing in the repository reads the VoiceOver state when choosing or warning about a shortcut: the only use of `isVoiceOverEnabled` is the dock presentation (`AppDelegate.swift:3322`).
**Root cause.** The default was chosen for people who do not use a screen reader, and the shortcut gate (`SettingsEditor.rejection`) knows about printable keys, Spotlight and the Globe key but has no notion of keys another assistive technology owns. The settle window is a fixed 200 ms, shorter than a deliberate VoiceOver chord.
**Design.** One data entry, "keys VoiceOver uses", read by the same gate that already refuses ⌥ with a character key. While VoiceOver is running: onboarding offers a different default (a key with a modifier, which the recogniser already supports) and explains why in one sentence; an existing install on the held ⌃⌥ default gets one informational notice with a one-step change; the settle for a binding made only of VoiceOver's modifiers is not shortened below a measured chord length. No new shortcut mechanism and no second recogniser.
**Acceptance.** A `HotkeyRecogniser` plus controller replay test of a one-second Control+Option hold followed by an arrow key: zero microphone opens, zero cues, zero announcements, with VoiceOver reported on. Onboarding with VoiceOver on never offers the held ⌃⌥ pair as the default (UI test). The probe result (how long a deliberate VoiceOver chord is held, measured on a real Mac with VoiceOver on) is recorded in `Docs/shortcuts.md`.
**Related.** #2443, #2471, CM.22, OP.32.

---
Part of #3351 (`initiative:dictation-quality`). Read AGENTS.md first, "No patchy fixes" and "One path per capability": the fix is the root cause and a clean seam, never a special case, and never a second implementation of the same job. Before and after are measured with `make bakeoff` or the transcription gate and written in the pull request. Companion audit: #232.

title: Extreme lag when VoiceOver is active

title: Improve VoiceOver labels for rewrite controls
body:
> Filed from `docs/main-integration-issues/11-improve-voiceover-labels.md` on branch `cloudai/build-rewrite-app-bd38`, where the brief and a reference implementation live.
>
> **Paths predate the pluma rename:** `Rewrite/…` is now `Pluma/…`, `RewriteTests/…` is now `PlumaTests/…`, and the project is `Pluma.xcodeproj`. Implement against current `main`, not the source branch.

Priority: Medium

## Summary

Add concise, state-aware accessibility labels to provider status, rewrite
errors, editable/result panels, and icon-only actions in the playground.

## Value

Several controls rely on icons, visual grouping, tooltips, or status colors.
VoiceOver users need equivalent names and state information without hearing
duplicated or excessively verbose content.

## Existing implementation to reuse

Source branch: `cloudai/build-rewrite-app-bd38`

- `Rewrite/Views/ProviderMenu.swift`
- `Rewrite/Views/RewritePlaygroundView.swift`
- Source commit: `012faea`

Existing additions include labels for:

- provider name, status, and status detail;
- rewrite failures;
- source/result editor regions;
- “Use result as original”;
- “Copy result”.

## Required implementation for `main`

1. Port the useful labels as small, reviewable SwiftUI changes.
2. Audit whether native controls already expose a sufficient label before
   overriding them.
3. Keep labels concise and avoid reading the entire rewritten result every time
   focus enters a large editor.
4. Expose changing provider/rewrite status as state or value where appropriate.
5. Ensure icon-only buttons have stable names independent of SF Symbol choice.
6. Group related decorative children without hiding interactive controls.
7. Review all three main pages—Rewrite, Autocomplete, and Dictation—for the same
   class of issue rather than limiting the audit to the playground.
8. Preserve Full Keyboard Access and visible focus behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every icon-only actionable control has a meaningful accessibility label.
- Provider selection communicates provider and readiness state.
- Errors are announced with context.
- Source and result regions are distinguishable.
- Large result text is not redundantly spoken by both a container and editor.
- Labels do not duplicate native button or picker names.
- Rewrite, Autocomplete, and Dictation pages are usable with VoiceOver and Full
  Keyboard Access.

## Verification

- Navigate the complete app using VoiceOver only.
- Repeat with Full Keyboard Access enabled.
- Verify light/dark appearance and increased contrast do not remove state cues.
- Test empty, loading, success, and error states.
- Use Accessibility Inspector to check names, roles, values, and grouping.

## Dependencies

None for the small label changes. Coordinate state labels with
`10-prevent-stale-rewrite-results.md`.

## Do not copy as-is

Review the source branch's combined result-container label before copying it.
Reading `model.outputText` as the container label can cause large results to be
spoken redundantly when the editor already exposes its value.

title: Accessibility + localization pass (zero VoiceOver support, no string catalog)
body:
The app has no VoiceOver support and no localization: zero `accessibilityLabel`/traits repo-wide, and every string is hardcoded English.

**Accessibility.** `accessibilityLabel` and `accessibilityAddTraits` have 0 matches across all Swift sources. The UI leans heavily on custom-drawn, non-standard controls, all of which are effectively invisible or unusable via VoiceOver:
- the status orb (conveys conversation state purely visually)
- the mic-level ring and waveform (no textual equivalent)
- gesture-driven controls, notably tap-to-end-turn (no discoverable action)

**Localization.** No `.xcstrings` catalog exists, despite `LOCALIZATION_PREFERS_STRING_CATALOGS = YES` being set in the project (`project.pbxproj:308`). All user-facing strings are inline literals.

**Why together:** both are mechanical once the scaffolding is in place, and both are gating items for public distribution — an App Store release with zero VoiceOver support on the primary control surface is a real review and usability risk.

**Fix:** add labels/values/traits to the orb, meters, waveform, and gesture controls (including an accessibility action for end-turn), then extract strings into a String Catalog.

**Effort:** M

---

From an external code review of this repo (`review-findings.md` / `improvement-plan.md` in the rowellr/mercury-voice fork). Line references re-verified against `main` on 2026-08-22.

title: Accessibility: expand abbreviations for VoiceOver and keep a chart-free path
body:
### What
Two things the accessibility standards for knit and crochet patterns ask for that we should check
ourselves against:

1. **Abbreviations must be expanded for screen readers.** "sc" is read as letters or as a word,
   and tech editors report screen readers rendering "st" as "street". Wherever the app is about
   to start showing a stitch abbreviation
   (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-12-pattern-data-model-design.md`), the VoiceOver label should
   say "single crochet" while the visible badge stays "sc". The spec already routes the
   accessibility label through `Stitch.name`; this issue is to check the rest of the app for the
   same problem and to add a guard test.
2. **A chart must never be the only path.** The standard guidance is "charts can be used, but
   full written instructions must also appear", and the BANA transcription guidelines let a
   transcriber convert a chart to written instructions row by row from the bottom when the chart
   is unwieldy. `written-rows.txt` is already that artifact — worth naming it as an
   accessibility guarantee in `docs/chart-format.md` so it does not get dropped, and worth making
   sure it stays complete as the turning chain and stitch land in it.

### Why
The Work screen is the whole product for a blind or low-vision user, and it is currently an
excellent shape for one — one big target, haptics, Dynamic Type, no chart required. Getting the
labels right is a small change that protects that.

### Rough size
Half a day, mostly auditing existing accessibility labels. The guard test can follow the shape of
`ios/Tests/DesignRulesTests.swift`.

### Waits on
Nothing. Best done with the stitch badge, since that is the change that introduces abbreviations
to the screen.

title: Marking prompt says "Tap the ac unit"
body:
On TestFlight build 1.1 (field test run 1, PR #23), marking the AC unit shows "Tap the ac unit". This is B-16 in the verification bug triage (`verification/product/bug-triage.md` on `t3/verification`).

**Cause.** `ScanCopy.markingPrompt` lowercases the feature name for every kind ([`ScanCopy.swift#L157`](https://github.com/SamGu-NRX/house-scanning-master/blob/e9e405d/ios/HouseScan/UI/Copy/ScanCopy.swift#L157), used at [L171-L172](https://github.com/SamGu-NRX/house-scanning-master/blob/e9e405d/ios/HouseScan/UI/Copy/ScanCopy.swift#L171-L172)), so "AC unit" becomes "ac unit". The same triage item notes that VoiceOver reads "Mark ac unit", and reads "ft" and "in" as letters.

**Fix.** Keep "AC" in capitals: give each kind its own mid-sentence noun instead of lowercasing. For VoiceOver, add accessibility labels that say "feet" and "inches".

title: VoiceOver focus read of the command line can speak a stale, already-submitted line
body:
On Command-2, VoiceOver's focus read of the command line sometimes speaks a previously submitted line instead of the empty input — heard as the old line's text followed by "Command line" (value, then label). The input is genuinely empty: the app cleared it on Return.

## Sightings

Two confirmed, both after content-heavy activity:

1. A single stray "l" spoken before "Command line", once, during the completion round-trip testing session. Not reproduced at the time.
2. A full previously-submitted command (a long pasted `gh issue view` line) spoken before "Command line". Reproduced deliberately with the recipe below.

## Reproduction recipe

The reliable sequence, each ingredient apparently necessary:

1. Command-2, paste a distinctive line into the input.
2. Review it with VoiceOver (arrow through it by character) — this is what puts the value in VoiceOver's cache.
3. Press Return to submit it.
4. Run a command that produces a long output burst.
5. Switch to another application and back.
6. Command-2. VoiceOver speaks the stale line, then "Command line".

A plain paste-submit-refocus without the review step and app switch did not reproduce it. The line spoken is the last one VoiceOver actually read while it sat in the input, not necessarily the last one submitted.

## Diagnosis

The value-then-label shape identifies this as VoiceOver's focus read serving a cached element value. The chain: VoiceOver caches the input's accessibility value whenever it reads the line; the app empties the line on submit but deliberately posts no value-changed notification (posting one on every keystroke would narrate typing, defeating the view-level input design); so nothing ever invalidates VoiceOver's cache; and a later focus read serves the stale value instead of refetching.

## Fix direction

Two changes, shipped together:

- Serve the accessibility value from an `accessibilityValue()` getter override instead of pushing it with `setAccessibilityValue` — a pushed value is stored state that can go stale; a getter can only answer with the current text. Same pattern the transcript view already uses for its quiet window.
- Post a single `.valueChanged` notification from `clear()` only — the one moment the line empties. The value at that moment is "", so there is nothing for VoiceOver to narrate, but the notification invalidates whatever it cached of the old line. Typing stays unnarrated because inserts still post nothing.

Verification is by ear: the recipe above with the fix applied, plus non-regression on typing silence, deletion announcements, and the completion round-trip's adopt path.

title: [BUG] Range needs VoiceOver support for alternating values
body:
- [x] I have written a [good issue](https://github.com/kirbydesign/designsystem/wiki/The-Good%3A-Issue) 

## Describe the bug
VoiceOver is only able to read out the current value of a Range slider. It would make sense to be able to programatically specify the text that is read out, eg. the value + a unit, or perhaps more advanced requirements for alternating texts.

## Describe how to reproduce the bug
1. Go to StackBlitz: https://stackblitz.com/edit/stackblitz-starters-wxb9gweu?file=src%2Fmain.ts
2. Ensure kirby-range [pin]='false' 
3. When adjusting the Range slider, only the new value is read out loud

## Which Kirby version was used?
10.2.1

## What was the expected behavior?
It would be much preferred if the component consuming the Range, could expose a function with logic that could report to the Range what was supposed to be read out by VoiceOver. Eg. "100.000 kr.", "30 shares" or "55.000 kr., higher than recommended".

## Add any screenshots
Sample screen recording, showing how the current [pinFormatter] is used to simulate the expected behaviour:
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/254e0ad5-09b5-44ec-b6f4-213f1085e1d7

## Please complete the following information:
- OS: macOS 15.2 with VoiceOver
- Browser: Google Chrome

## Are there any additional context?
I suggest a new optional callback is offered by the Range component, eg. [ariaSliderAdjustCallback]="someFunction", which will allow the consuming component, to decide the text read out by VoiceOver, based on the current value of the slider. Very much like the [pinFormatter] works. 

In the StackBlitz mentioned above, set kirby-range [pin]='true', to get an idea of what kind of flexibility we wish for when using VoiceOver (think of the values shown in the Pin, as values that would instead be read out to the user). In this case it doesn't make sense to show the text in a pin, as it is rather long, but make perfect sense when being read out loud.

title: [EuiFlyout] Title is not announced in VoiceOver on Chrome
body:
**Reported by**

@seialkali 

**Describe the bug**
When using `EuiFlyout` with `aria-labelledby` set to the flyout heading (as recommended in the EUI docs), the flyout title is not announced by VoiceOver in Chrome when the flyout opens. Instead, only the `aria-describedby` text (e.g. “You are in a non-modal dialog…”) is announced.

This behavior also occurs in the [EUI Flyout examples in the docs](https://eui.elastic.co/docs/components/containers/flyout/). As a result, screen reader users do not hear the flyout title announced on open in Chrome + VoiceOver, even though the title is visually present and programmatically associated via `aria-labelledby`.

**Impact and severity**
**End-user impact:** Yes
**Severity**: Moderate accessibility issue.

Screen reader users (specifically VoiceOver users in Chrome) do not get the flyout title announced on entry, which makes it harder to understand context (e.g. “Create rule”, “Edit rule”) when the flyout opens.

Even when tabbing through the content in the flyout, any header content seems to get skipped and only the body content is announced, so users may never hear the flyout title announced.

**Workaround**:
Setting `aria-label` directly on `EuiFlyout` causes the label to be announced immediately, but this duplicates visible text and diverges from the documented recommendation to use `aria-labelledby`.

**Environment and versions**
- **EUI version**: Latest 
- **Browser**: Chrome
- **Operating System**: macOS
- **Assistive Technology**: VoiceOver

**To Reproduce**

1) Open Chrome on macOS
2) Navigate to the [flyout docs page](https://eui.elastic.co/docs/components/containers/flyout/)
3) Enable VoiceOver
4) Open any flyout example
5) Listen to the announcement when the flyout opens and you should notice that the flyout title is not announced

**Expected behavior**
When the flyout opens, VoiceOver should announce the flyout title referenced by `aria-labelledby` (e.g. “Create rule”) along with the dialog role.

**Additional context (Optional)**
Findings by @tkajtoch in [this Slack thread](https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C7QC1JV6F/p1769092431949459):

Based on [this answer](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/13224#issuecomment-1009913977) to an NVDA issue on this topic, it's likely an expected behavior, because the element referenced in `aria-labelledby` would be read anyway with moving through the page. It might be a way to deduplicate read information.

When `aria-label` is set on `EuiFlyout` it gets announced straight away.

From what I can see, JAWS, NVDA and Safari with VoiceOver can all properly see the flyout title text and read it when navigating through the flyout content. Chrome with VoiceOver seems to ignore the flyout title text, though, which I believe is the reason why this a11y issue got created. I believe this might be a bug in Chrome, but so far I haven't found any external issues that would make it clear.

It’s also worth noting that the spec says that these would not be announced if the element is non-interactive, as non-modals (and our non-push flyouts) are. If that’s the reasoning of chrome, I don’t know why it would read the content of the Flyout but ignore the title…

title: Post-merge follow-ups from the NVDA accessibility remediation
body:
## Issue Description

Four follow-ups were recorded when PR #2934 merged. This issue tracks them together. Three are repairs; one is a disposition recorded so it is not mistaken for unfinished work.

PR #2934 is referenced only as the origin of these items. Its review findings are closed and are not reopened here.

## 1. OWASP citations are dead (repair)

OWASP restructured its site from `owasp.org/www-project-<slug>` to `owasp.org/projects/<slug>`. The repository contains 8 distinct legacy URLs across 17 files, concentrated in the OWASP security skills.

Two are confirmed 404:

- `https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/`
- `https://owasp.org/www-project-ai-security-and-privacy-guide/`

The remaining six are unverified, not known-good. The CI link check runs with `changed-files-only: true` and `soft-fail: true`, so it neither inspects nor blocks on files that rarely change.

**Done when:** every one of the 8 URLs has been individually checked, each replacement is confirmed to resolve *and* to be the same OWASP project the original cited, and any URL without a confirmed replacement is left unchanged and listed here as a named exception. No slug is inferred from a pattern.

## 2. Word-stem dictionary is oversized and its rationale is false (repair)

`.cspell/word-stems.txt` holds 139 fragments. Its header claims a stem such as `compl` accepts any token beginning with it. That is false: a probe of `validatxyz complzzz conformaqqq` reports all three as unknown words. cspell matches whole words here.

The entries also do not share one origin. At least three sources exist:

- truncated generated grader names, for example `...-signal-compl-a5d0ffac`
- hand-authored identifiers, for example `per-stim` in `docs/contributing/evals-ci.md` and `prereq.json` in the accessibility runbook
- hand-authored regex fragments, for example `(?is)(revalidat|validat|check)` in `evals/agent-behavior/stimuli/code-review.yml`

Because of that, the file cannot simply be deleted, and renaming graders would not help: the truncated names are committed identities pinned by `evals/migrations/vally-0.16-grader-name-aliases.json`, so regenerating them would register as lineage drift.

**Done when:** every entry is attributed to its actual source, entries with no remaining occurrence are removed, generated-name entries are covered by a scoping mechanism, genuinely hand-authored entries are retained, the header states something true, and a deliberate typo in ordinary prose is still reported.

## 3. Announcement coalescing has no runtime evidence (repair)

Walkthrough step announcements are coalesced behind a 150 ms settle timer so a superseded step does not speak. Both the shipped and starter decks implement it and both assert it only in source text. `docs/docusaurus/e2e/slides.spec.ts` asserts slide-change announcements only.

This is the behavior most likely to regress silently, because it is timing-dependent.

**Done when:** a browser assertion advances the walkthrough faster than the settle delay and observes a single settled announcement, and that assertion is proven to fail when the timer is removed rather than assumed to work.

## 4. `_intent.py` POSIX gate: no change proposed (disposition)

`_require_secure_write_support` requires POSIX `dir_fd`, `O_DIRECTORY`, and `O_NOFOLLOW`, so 49 of 84 tests in `test_intent.py` fail on Windows locally.

**This is not a coverage gap.** The `Python Tests (.github/skills/accessibility/accessibility)` lane runs on Linux and reported `600 passed`, which reconciles exactly with the 516 that run locally plus the 84 intent tests. CI executes all of them.

Relaxing the precondition would weaken a deliberate security control for local convenience. Recorded here so the earlier "49 tests unexecuted" note is not misread as missing coverage.

**Disposition:** no change proposed. Close this item with the record, not a fix.

## Additional Context

- Also open, a

title: Month navigation: "Next Month" can stop working, and there is no way back
body:
### Describe the bug - [ ] **"Next Month" does not change the month when the Query block has `queryId` 0** (important before merge) - [ ] Screen readers do not hear the new month after "Next Month" - [ ] Visitors cannot go back before the first month ### Steps to Reproduce Each item below has its own steps and code references. Open an item to see them.
1. "Next Month" does not change the month when queryId is 0 **What happens:** "Next Month" opens `?query-0-page=2`, but the calendar still shows the same month. The block editor gives `queryId: 0` to the first Query block it creates in a session, so this is common. **Steps:** 1. Create a new page and insert the "Event Calendar" block. Publish it. 2. The saved markup has `"queryId":0`. 3. On the page, click "Next Month". **Expected:** The next month is shown. **Actual:** The URL changes and "Previous Month" appears, but the grid still shows the same month. **Code:** `includes/classes/class-calendar.php:95` and `includes/classes/class-setup.php:250`: `$page_key = $query_id > 0 ? "query-{$query_id}-page" : 'query-page';` WordPress core uses `'query-' . $queryId . '-page'` when `queryId` is set, and 0 counts (`wp-includes/blocks/query-pagination-next.php:22`). `class-query-builder.php:42` already does it the core way. With another `queryId`, navigation works. **Fix idea:** Use `"query-{$query_id}-page"` when the Query block has a `queryId`, including 0.
2. Screen readers do not hear the new month **What happens:** After "Next Month", NVDA says "Loading page, please wait." and then nothing. Focus moves to the page body. The user does not know that the calendar now shows October. See `nvda-frontend.json` (`nextPhrase`, `afterNext`). **Code:** This is the default behavior of core's enhanced pagination (`enhancedPagination: true` in `src/calendar/variation.js:28`). **Fix idea:** After navigation, announce the new month in a polite live region, or move focus to the month heading.
3. Visitors cannot go back before the first month **What happens:** The calendar starts on the current month. There is no "Previous Month" link, so visitors cannot see last month's events. **Code:** Page 1 is always the start month, and core pagination has no page 0. **Question:** Is this by design? If past months should be available, the start month could be a page in the middle, or the calendar could use its own month parameter.
### Screenshots, screen recording, code snippet Image are inline above. NVDA output in nvda-frontend.json (first review, 6e07c5a) is linked below. [nvda-frontend.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32805742/nvda-frontend.json) ### Environment information - Device: Windows PC - OS: Windows 11 Pro - Browser and version: Chromium 153 and Firefox 155, driven by Playwright - Screen reader: NVDA 2026.2 with Firefox. The NVDA quotes are from the first review (commit 6e07c5a); on 47302fe I re-checked these items in the browser and in the code. ### WordPress information - WordPress 7.1 - PHP 8.2 - GatherPress: develop branch (commit a71ad481) - Theme: GatherPress org theme 2.0 - GatherPress Calendar: commit 47302fe (0.5.0)

title: Add accessibility testing support to the web module (axe first, screen readers later) a11y
body:
## Problem

ATAF can run Selenium and Cucumber UI tests, but it has no shared accessibility **a11y** support. Suites that depend on the `web` module cannot easily check for common accessibility problems or build on a common approach later for screen-reader related checks.

There are three widely used screen readers in practice. **JAWS** is the commercial industry standard on Windows. **NVDA** is the free Windows alternative and a common choice for testing. **VoiceOver** is built into Apple platforms (Mac, iPhone, and related devices). They do not behave identically, so accessibility work usually means covering more than one of them over time rather than treating “screen reader” as a single tool.

## What we want

Add accessibility support to the `web` module in small steps, using the same Cucumber style as existing `@web` scenarios. New steps would live in `ataf.web.steps` so consumer suites keep their current glue setup.

The first step is **axe-core**: an open-source rules engine from Deque that inspects a page (DOM / accessibility tree) and reports many WCAG-related issues such as missing labels, contrast problems, or incorrect roles. It does not run a real screen reader and does not tell you what JAWS, NVDA, or VoiceOver would speak. It is the practical automated baseline for CI.

In ATAF, axe-core would run through Selenium after normal navigation. A scenario could look like this:

```gherkin
@web @a11y @smoke
Szenario: Startseite ohne kritische Barrieren
  Wenn Sie die URL "https://example.muenchen.de" aufrufen.
  Dann sollte die Seite keine Accessibility-Verletzungen mit Impact "critical" haben.
```

The last step would run axe on the current page, fail if matching violations are found, and attach a short report to the Cucumber output. Configuration would use simple `testautomation.a11y.*` properties.

A second step can add keyboard and focus helpers, still inside Selenium and Cucumber. That covers things axe often misses, such as tab order and where focus lands after Tab or Shift+Tab:

```gherkin
@web @a11y
Szenario: Tab-Reihenfolge im Login-Formular
  Wenn Sie die URL "https://example.muenchen.de/login" aufrufen.
  Wenn Sie 1 Mal die Tabulatortaste drücken.
  Dann sollte der Fokus auf dem Element "#username" liegen.
  Wenn Sie 1 Mal die Tabulatortaste drücken.
  Dann sollte der Fokus auf dem Element "#password" liegen.
```

A further step would be real screen-reader automation (what users actually hear). That should stay outside the Java ATAF module and use something like Guidepup for NVDA and VoiceOver. In GitHub Actions this can be prepared with the third-party [Guidepup Setup](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/guidepup-setup) Marketplace action (published by Guidepup, not an official GitHub-built action). Reader-specific tags would select the right OS runner. JAWS would stay manual or exploratory unless a maintained automation path appears.

```gherkin
@nvda
Szenario: Hauptnavigation mit NVDA
  Wenn die Seite "https://example.muenchen.de" geladen ist.
  Wenn NVDA zur nächsten Überschrift springt.
  Dann sollte NVDA "Willkommen" ansagen.
```

## Done when (first step)

A `@web @a11y` scenario can fail on configured axe impacts, the violation summary is attached to the Cucumber report, behaviour is configurable via `testautomation.a11y.*`, and the handbook briefly documents how to use it.

## Out of scope for now

Rewriting ATAF around Playwright, making JAWS a default CI gate, or embedding screen-reader drivers in Java.

## References

[Screen readers overview](https://tigertracks.isu.edu/TDClient/1950/Portal/KB/Article/168886/Screen-Reader-JAWS-NVDA-VoiceOver) · [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) · [Guidepup](https://www.guidepup.dev/) · [Guidepup Setup action](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/guidepup-setup)

This context reaches the children before the `BlockContextProvider` in `src/calendar-day/edit.js`. title: Accessibility Regression: NVDA mouse tracking broken due to Chromium 142 update (Upstream Issue)
body: Type: Bug Description Since the recent VS Code update bumped the internal Chromium version to 142 (from 138), the "Mouse Tracking" feature in the NVDA screen reader has stopped working completely within the editor. This is a known regression in Chromium starting from version 140. It affects all Chromium-based applications. According to the NVDA issue tracker, this bug has been identified and fixed in Chromium 144 (currently in Canary), but versions between 140 and 143 remain broken. Impact This is a significant accessibility blocker. Users who rely on NVDA mouse tracking to explore the UI or read code by hovering are currently unable to use this feature, severely hampering navigation and productivity. Steps to Reproduce Launch NVDA (ensure mouse tracking is enabled in NVDA settings). Open VS Code (running on Chromium 142). Move the mouse cursor over the editor text, sidebar, or any UI element. Actual Behavior: NVDA stays silent and does not read the element under the mouse. Expected Behavior: NVDA should read the element under the mouse cursor. Root Cause & Evidence This is not an NVDA bug, but a Chromium regression introduced in v140. NVDA Issue Reference: nvaccess/nvda#18707 and nvaccess/nvda#18996 Chromium Status: The issue comments confirm: "This has been fixed in chrome canary (144)." Proposed Solution / Request Given that Chromium 144 is not yet stable, we kindly request the VS Code team to consider: Rolling back the internal Chromium/Electron version to a build based on Chromium 138 (or any pre-140 version) where this feature was stable. Alternatively, applying a specific patch if possible until Chromium 144 becomes the stable base for Electron/VS Code. title: app: parar de reconstruir o DOM inteiro a cada render
body:
## Causa

`render()` faz `app.innerHTML = ...` (`app/src/main.js:263`). `vote()` chama `render()` quatro vezes por rodada. Toda a subárvore é destruída e recriada, e com ela o foco do teclado e as regiões `aria-live`.

Esta é a raiz arquitetural de três barreiras de acessibilidade ao mesmo tempo. Tratá-las separadamente produz três remendos que brigam entre si.

## Evidência medida

```
MutationObserver em #app:  4 trocas completas de subárvore por voto
document.activeElement:    BODY nas quatro

região role="status":
  mesmoNóDeAntes      false
  nóAntigoAindaNoDom  false
```

Consequências: quem navega por teclado volta ao topo do documento a cada escolha e precisa re-tabular, sempre para a carta 1. E uma região `aria-live` inserida já com o conteúdo dentro não dispara anúncio — o resultado do voto provavelmente nunca chega ao leitor de tela.

> O item do leitor de tela é **inferido** do comportamento do DOM, não observado. Confirmar com NVDA ou VoiceOver antes de dar como fechado.

## O que NÃO resolve

- Guardar o seletor do elemento focado e refocar depois do render. É remendo: o cursor virtual do leitor de tela continua resetando, e o `aria-live` continua não anunciando.
- Marcar `tabindex="-1"` em coisas para "arrumar" a ordem.
- Mover o `role="status"` de lugar sem parar de recriá-lo.

## Pronto quando

- [x] As regiões que precisam persistir (`.round-instruction`, a nav, a topbar) deixam de ser recriadas: o render passa a atualizar texto e atributos dos nós existentes.
- [x] O foco do teclado sobrevive a um voto — medido com `document.activeElement` antes e depois.
- [ ] Um voto completo é anunciado por leitor de tela real (NVDA ou VoiceOver). Anexar o que foi ouvido.
- [x] Sem regressão no `app/e2e/interaction-smoke.mjs` e no `vote-recovery.mjs`.

Parte do portão de qualidade para `main`.

## Triagem após a mesclagem da #205 — 17/09/2026

**Manter aberta — falta evidência de leitor de tela real.** Persistência dos nós, foco e regressões já passaram em Chromium/WebKit. Próximo passo: executar uma rodada com NVDA ou VoiceOver e anexar versão do leitor/navegador, anúncios de confirmação/resultado/nova rodada e comportamento do cursor virtual. Esta é também a pendência assistiva remanescente do trabalho de teclado da #167, encerrada por seus critérios técnicos; não se declara escuta assistiva realizada.

Base técnica: [PR #205](https://github.com/stefancabral-oss/presidencia-duelo/pull/205), merge `f99ac18`; [CI de navegador](https://github.com/stefancabral-oss/presidencia-duelo/actions/runs/35186478148) e [CI backend/shared/PostgreSQL](https://github.com/stefancabral-oss/presidencia-duelo/actions/runs/35186478145) aprovados. Esta triagem não registra aprovação humana inexistente.

title: Accessibility: app region is announced as disabled (host container has aria-disabled="true")
body:
## Problem
Twenty renders the app's page-layout widget inside a container with `aria-disabled="true"`. Buttons and inputs inside work with mouse, touch and keyboard, but assistive technology may announce the whole region as disabled, and automated tools (e.g. Playwright) treat every control as disabled.

This comes from Twenty's host code, not from this app (see "Known limitations" in CHANGELOG.md).

## Scope
1. Reproduce with a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver or Orca) on the Now screen and record what is announced.
2. Check whether a widget/page-layout setting in `twenty-sdk` avoids it.
3. If not, open an issue upstream in https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty with a minimal reproduction and link it here.
4. Run an accessibility checker (axe DevTools or Lighthouse) on the app and list findings that *are* in this repository's code (`src/ui/**`).

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Findings documented in this issue (announced text, tool output).
- [x] Upstream issue linked, or a fix in this repository if one is possible.
- [x] Separate issues opened for app-side findings.

## Not in scope
Redesigning the UI.

title: Accessibility audit and remediation for financial data tables and transaction history views
body:
## Overview
The credit marketplace tables, transaction history, and portfolio views are not screen-reader accessible and fail WCAG 2.1 AA at multiple points: missing table headers with `scope`, numeric data without units in accessible labels, interactive rows with no keyboard focus management, and status badges with color-only differentiation. Conduct a full audit using axe-core and NVDA/VoiceOver, then remediate all critical and serious violations.

## Scope
**In scope:**
- Automated audit with axe-core integrated into CI (failing build on new violations)
- Manual audit with at least one screen reader (NVDA on Windows or VoiceOver on macOS)
- Remediation of all critical and serious WCAG 2.1 AA violations
- Keyboard navigation for all interactive table rows and modals

**Out of scope:**
- WCAG 2.2 or AAA compliance
- Mobile screen reader testing (iOS VoiceOver)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] axe-core integrated into CI; zero critical or serious violations on all audited pages
- [ ] All data tables have correct `<th scope>` attributes and ARIA labels for numeric columns including units (e.g., "12.5 tCO₂e")
- [ ] Status badges communicate state via text or `aria-label`, not color alone
- [ ] All modals trap focus correctly and return focus to the triggering element on close
- [ ] A `docs/accessibility/audit-report.md` documents the initial audit findings, severity, and the remediation applied

## Complexity
**High**

## Estimated Time Frame
2–3 weeks (part-time contributor)

## Relevant Files / Contracts
`frontend/`, `app/investor/`, `components/`

title: Excess speech feedback when using JAWS screen reader
body:
### Your idea

The speech feedback using JAWS is excessive, redundant, and makes workflow inefficient

### Problem to be solved

Is there a way of controlling how much speech feedback the user receives when using a screen reader? I didn't see any setting under Preferences for controlling this.

As an example, here is the speech feedback I got from JAWS when arrowing to a particular measure and beat in my project:

"Measure 10, Measure 10
Segment, Measure 10 Beat 3
Chord, Measure 10 Beat 3
Note A flat 4 Quarter, , Measure 10 Beat 3"

There is obviously a lot of redundant feedback here. The speech feedback not only takes too long to listen to if one wants to work efficiently, but it also masks the key information that I would like to hear, i.e., the note and duration.

There is also useless information in the feedback. For example, there is no variable "segment" information. Also, there are no "chords" just single "notes". So perhaps those announcements can be removed.

Another thought to help minimize the amount of speech while still providing the user with key information is to only speak items that have changed since the last navigation command was given. For example, If I arrow to measure one beat 1 and then arrow to beat 2 of the same measure, I am obviously in measure 1 and don't need to hear "mesure 1 beat 1" again since "beat 2" would be sufficient.

Perhaps there could be some settings added to the preferences (maybe under an "Accessibility" category?) in which each user could specify how much feedback is desired. This might include what types of items are spoken, whether information that has not changed is spoken or not, etc.

When the braille support becomes more robust for JAWS, I would also hope that the same philosophy can be applied to what is displayed in braille since most braille displays have limited real estate to show braille (usually 40 characters for most displays and no more than 80 for the high end displays).  Additionally, using abbreviations like "m:' and "B:" for measure and beat would save a lot of braille real estate to ensure that information can fit on the braille display.

--Pete

Follow-up to #2104 and #2116. ## Goal Let `triggerWhenObjectsClicked` fire for ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, `` and `` outside a graph, as #2116 did for ``, ``, `

Click x^2 to see its derivative.

``` ## Where things stand - **The worker side is ready.** - `Math.js`, `MMeMen.js` and `MdMdnMrow.js` already have `mathClicked`, which calls `triggerChainedActions` when the component isn't `fixed`. - What's missing is a call to `addClickTargetStateVariableDefinition` in each (`utils/triggering.js`), so the renderer knows something listens. - **The renderer side is the open question.** - All of these use `math.tsx`. - #2116's `ClickTargetButton` (`renderers/utils/ClickTarget.tsx`) is a ``. - ARIA treats a button's children as presentational, so MathJax's assistive MathML would be flattened. A screen reader would lose the structure of the math. ## To decide, by testing with NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver - Give the button an `aria-label` from MathJax's speech text. `DynamicMath` doesn't expose it yet. - Or keep the math outside the button, and point the button's name at it with `aria-labelledby`. - Display math (``, ``) is a block. Decide how a clickable display equation should look and where its focus ring goes. - `` with embedded inputs (`MathWithEmbeddedInputs`) contains live controls, so it can't be a click target. It should render plain, like other nested controls. ## Notes from #2116 - `clickTarget.css` already draws a dotted bottom border under inline `mjx-container`, because `text-decoration` doesn't reach into MathJax's inline-blocks. - `useMathJaxOutOfTabOrder` already keeps MathJax's own tab stops out of a click target. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Error messages and NetworkBanner have no aria-live region for screen readers
body:
## Problem `src/screens/ConnectScreen.tsx` and `src/components/TopBar.tsx` both render error messages in a `

` tag without `role="alert"`. When an error occurs (e.g., wallet connect failure), the error text updates in the DOM, but screen readers will not automatically announce the new content because there is no live region. A second related problem: `src/components/NetworkBanner.tsx` renders a colored banner that changes when the network switches, but has no `role="status"` or `aria-live` attribute, so the change goes unannounced. Both of these are silent for assistive technology users — they would see no visual change (on screen readers) and receive no notification that something important happened. ## Solution 1. Add `role="alert"` to error `

` elements in `ConnectScreen.tsx` and `TopBar.tsx`. This implicitly sets `aria-live="assertive"`. 2. Add `role="status"` and `aria-live="polite"` to the `NetworkBanner` container so network switches are announced without interrupting the user. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] Error paragraph in `ConnectScreen.tsx` has `role="alert"` - [ ] Error banner in `TopBar.tsx` has `role="alert"` - [ ] `NetworkBanner.tsx` container has `role="status"` and `aria-live="polite"` - [ ] Screen reader (NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver) announces errors immediately when they appear - [ ] Network banner changes are announced politely without interrupting speech --- > **Note for Contributors:** If you are assigned to this issue, write a clear and detailed description for your pull request. Explain what was changed, why it was needed, how it was implemented, and include any relevant testing or screenshots where applicable.

title: SPIKE: Improve experience for creating annotations/highlights with NVDA (and JAWS)
body:
## Overview
When using VoiceOver for Mac to annotate, VoiceOver will read out the text that is being selected, whether that's character-by-character, or word-by-word. You can see this in action here: 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AOyVt1w_MUU

I have worked extensively with two users who are blind and experienced with NVDA and JAWS, and they have worked with each other to try and replicate this workflow in NVDA and JAWS with no success. The short version: text selection with NVDA and JAWS happens in an invisible text layer that the Hypothesis client doesn't see. When text is selected, the annotation adder doesn't appear. When NVDA or JAWS users interact directly with the page, they can create text selections but there is no audio feedback

## Research and troubleshooting
Here is a summary of our findings thus far:

- Reading a web page with NVDA typically happens in what is called Browse Mode. This is an invisible text layer, and interaction with the text (e.g., making a selection to copy and paste) does not happen within the DOM, and is invisible to the Hypothesis client. 
- When reading a web page with JAWS, navigation through the page happens in an invisible text layer using the Virtual Cursor rather than on the document itself. If a user wants to copy and paste a passage of text, they make the text selection in this invisible text layer. Nothing is happening within the DOM here, and this is invisible to the Hypothesis client. 
- NVDA and JAWS do allow for direct interaction with the contents of web pages— this is necessary for things like filling out forms, pressing buttons, etc. In NVDA this is called Focus Mode. In JAWS, this is called Forms Mode. 
- In both NVDA and JAWS, I was able to help users activate caret browsing (as seen in the VoiceOver video) to navigate through the text on the screen and create text selections. However, neither screenreader provides audio feedback while text is being selected, so a blind user has no idea what they are highlighting. Making this even more confusing is the fact that switching between Browse and Focus mode doesn't necessarily mean the cursors will be in the same place. So I might be in the middle of a document in Browse mode, switch to Focus mode to annotate, and the cursor takes me back up to the beginning of the text and I have to find the passage I want to annotate again. 
- The users I have been working with reached out to the NVDA support forum and to the support team for Vispero (the vendor that makes JAWS), and neither resource was able to help. 
- I looked into how Google Docs handles text selection for their commenting function. [Their documentation](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6239410) indicates that a comment can only be added to one word. This would be a better experience for our NVDA and JAWS users than the current one, but still not ideal (as sighted users and blind users on VoiceOver are able to expand text selections to entire passages, or narrow them to one character). 

## Helpful documentation
 - [Browse and Focus modes for screenreaders](https://www.accessibility-developer-guide.com/knowledge/screen-readers/desktop/browse-focus-modes/)
- [Navigating a web page with NVDA](https://webaim.org/articles/nvda/)
- [Discussion on NVDA support forum re: selecting text](https://nvda.groups.io/g/nvda/topic/76127378#76270)
- [Copying and pasting with NVDA](https://nvda.groups.io/g/nvda/topic/copying_an_pasting_with_nvda/3296978?p=)
- [Navigating a web page with JAWS](https://www.freedomscientific.com/SurfsUp/Navigating.htm#:~:text=JAWS%20Tip%3A%20To%20begin%20reading,Then%20use%20normal%20reading%20keys.)
- [Selecting text with JAWS](https://doccenter.freedomscientific.com/doccenter/doccenter/rs11f929e9c511/2015-02-26_teacherstrainers-l8/02_SelectingTextCutCopyAndPaste.htm)
- [Adding comments to a Google Doc with a screen reader ](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6239410)

Since it's "GPT4**All**", making the desktop applications accessible should hopefully be a big priority :)

GPT4All was tested for minimum functional accessibility using a Windows computer and JAWS screenreader. The following accessibility issues were identified:

Accessibility testing indicates that GPT4All is likely to present accessibility barriers to some individuals with disabilities.

  - Expected Outcome: Should be able to read all text, links, buttons, etc.

title: Cannot use JAWS or other screen-readers with many pages
body:
Trello commenter "@Bookrage" mentioned some accessibility issues for the blind and I asked for some more information. He sent me a more complete writeup of what working.

I use JAWS (Jaws Accessibility With Speech.” One of the two big screenreader programs for Windows and I use Internet Explorer 11 as my browser. (Jaws works okay with Firefox but it actually handles Habitica better with IE oddly enough and is terrible with Chrome.)

In regards to habits, there are a number of problems. First, the buttons involved are just interpereted as checkboxes and when I click on them (with keyboard commands or using an aspect of Jaws called the Jaws Cursor where you control the mouse with the keyboard, it simply check and unchecks the + and – buttons and clicking them again just unchecks them, doing nothing. Also, it is impossible to tell one checkbox from the other so if it did do something, a player using Jaws could easily select weak outcomes rather than strong ones and hurt themselves when they in fact deserve to be rewarded. There is no real reference point since the up and down arrows move people around a site based on the site itself. If I knew which box Jaws came to first, it wouldn’t be a problem.

Also, most buttons on pages are not labeled. These buttons will make Jaws say things like “unlabeled 4 button) or unlabled 1 button. Also, as things stand it doesn’t usually read item icons. The only way I can equip things is remembering exactly what order I got stuff in since all of them just say “unlabeled 1 button) when you have the Jaws cursor focused on them. This is also true for everything in every shop and every pet in both eggs, pets, and mounts. I have to get a sighted person to help me right now.

I can tell you now in regards to the rewards section of the tasks page, the way you purchase something with Jaws is have your cursor sitting on the cost of said item and pressing enter, though I haven’t found a reliable way to look at stats of things before I buy them.

title: [progress][meter] accessibility: NVDA and JAWS don't announce the programmatic label
body:
# Bug report

## Current behavior

Unfortunately, screen reader support for the progress and meter roles is still quite inconsistent. 

During testing, both NVDA and JAWS announced "Progress bar #%"  and did not announce the visible label that is referenced using `aria-labelledby`. This makes the progress bars lose all meaning because they are not labelled.

## Expected behavior

Progress bar programmatic (and visible) labels should be announced by screen readers. 

Although I suspect this may be a problem with the screen readers themselves, the current experience will be very poor for people using a screen reader when they encounter this BaseUI component, particularly if, for example, several meter components are used on a page, each with distinct labels.

## Reproducible example

Steps to reproduce: 
1. Navigate to the [Meter component demo](https://base-ui.com/react/components/meter)
2. Turn on either NVDA or JAWS on Windows
3. Use the Arrow keys to move through the component demo (reading mode)
4. Note the progress bar role and value is announced without announcing the visible label of "Storage used"
5. Test again with VoiceOver on mac and note the difference. The visible label is announced as expected along with the role and value.

## Base UI version

v1.2.0

## Which browser are you using?

Chrome

## Which OS are you using?

Windows

## Which assistive tech are you using (if applicable)?

NVDA and JAWS

## Additional context

Making the element with `role="meter"` focusable using `tabindex="0"` would fix the announcement and improve this, even though this is not meant to be a focusable element. In this case, this would be a valid improvement, as the minor trade-off of an extra tab stop would fix a serious issue for two widely used screen readers.

title: Audit TalkBack focus, semantics, and touch targets in the default flow
body:
## Context

BlindAssist is intended for blind and low-vision users, so accessibility of the default interaction flow is a product requirement rather than cosmetic polish. The audit should cover actual TalkBack behavior, not only static labels.

## Scope

- Audit launch, camera permission, main assist flow, settings, error/recovery states, and any persistent controls.
- Check Compose semantics, accessible names/roles/states, traversal order, focus restoration, announcements, touch targets, contrast, and non-gesture alternatives.
- Capture Android version, device or emulator profile, font/display scale, and TalkBack version with the evidence.
- Keep experimental/research-only screens separate from claims about the default flow.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reproducible screen-by-screen audit checklist is committed.
- [ ] Every actionable failure has a focused regression test where the Android test surface supports it.
- [ ] Remaining manual-only checks include device/TalkBack evidence and a clear owner.
- [ ] Critical controls meet the repository's touch-target and semantic requirements.
- [ ] No result is described as a user-safety or independent-mobility certification.

## Suggested contribution slices

Contributors can take one bounded screen or one failure class at a time. Please include before/after evidence and the exact validation command in the PR.

title: Accessibility review
body:
Ave should work well with VoiceOver and TalkBack, large text settings, and keyboards.

A good first pass:
- Pray a full rosary with a screen reader on, and note anything that is not announced clearly.
- Check every button has a clear label (the bead stage, the theme switch, the booklet controls).

title: Native nightly: accessibility-tree lint from Maestro hierarchy dumps, report-only
body:
Part of the CI build-out (see the tracking issue). **Nightly and report-only.** Builds on the native flows issue.

## Why

Jest checks accessible names on the React tree, not what VoiceOver and TalkBack actually receive. Xcode's `performAccessibilityAudit` and Android's Accessibility Test Framework need native test targets, which fight Continuous Native Generation. Maestro can already dump the native accessibility tree, so a script can check that instead.

## What

- At each key screen in the native flows, capture the view hierarchy (`maestro hierarchy` or the flow's equivalent output).
- A script in `scripts/`, covered by `npm run test:scripts`, reads the dumps and reports:
  - tappable elements with no accessible text;
  - tap targets smaller than 44×44 pt on iOS or 48×48 dp on Android;
  - duplicate accessible names on one screen that make controls ambiguous.
- An allowlist file holds known, accepted exceptions, each with a reason.
- Findings go into the nightly's artifact and the same report issue as the screenshot diffs. The nightly does not fail on them.

## Done when

- The checker runs for every flow at default and maximum text size on both platforms.
- A deliberately unlabeled button is reported.
- `docs/accessibility.md` describes the check and its limits: it does not replace a screen-reader pass.

title: [P1][Validation] Verify WCAG 2.2 AA with automation and assistive technology
body:
## Outcome

Verify WCAG 2.2 AA across all page templates, interactive states, viewport modes, and critical assistive-technology journeys.

## Current evidence and gap

The repository already checks serious/critical axe violations, skip links, tab semantics, visible focus, 44-pixel targets, reduced motion, 320-pixel reflow, Mermaid alternatives, and a dated VoiceOver/Safari pass. The validation program must refresh this evidence against the full current surface and add state, browser, zoom, and assistive-technology coverage that automation cannot prove.

## Scope

- Run axe against every unique template and meaningful state, including loading, empty, validation error, provider outage, signed-out save, signed-in save, quiz feedback, search results, mobile copilot, workshop, owner comments, and rendered/fallback Mermaid.
- Verify semantic landmarks, heading order, labels/instructions, status/live regions, table/code semantics, link purpose, error identification, and text alternatives.
- Complete keyboard-only journeys for global navigation, search combobox, mobile dialog/focus trap, tabs, quizzes, notes/comments, checklist controls, diagram editor, workshop canvas, and owner actions.
- Verify focus order/restoration/visibility, no keyboard traps, skip behavior, pointer alternatives, target size, drag alternatives, and timeout behavior.
- Test 200% text zoom, 400% browser zoom/320 CSS-pixel reflow, landscape, high contrast/forced colors where available, reduced motion, and contrast in every status/control state.
- Perform manual screen-reader runs on VoiceOver with Safari/macOS and at least one additional materially different stack such as NVDA with Firefox/Chrome or VoiceOver on iOS; record unavailable hardware as blocked, not passed.
- Verify dynamic search, save, error, chat, quiz, and diagram announcements without excessive or transcript-wide live-region noise.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No critical or serious axe violation exists across the declared template/state matrix.
- [ ] All critical journeys complete by keyboard alone with visible focus and correct focus restoration.
- [ ] Zoom, reflow, contrast, forced-color/reduced-motion, target-size, and orientation checks meet WCAG 2.2 AA expectations.
- [ ] Screen-reader evidence covers navigation, reader content, search, learning lab, chat, workshop, persistence errors, and owner comments.
- [ ] Mermaid diagrams and complex tables/code remain understandable without vision.
- [ ] The accessibility release record lists OS, browser, AT versions, date, commit, routes, results, limitations, and artifacts.
- [ ] No unresolved P0/P1 accessibility defect remains.

- Automated reports plus a manual assistive-technology record with sanitized screenshots/video or structured notes.

Depends on the validation evidence-matrix issue. Coordinate browser/device coverage with the cross-browser issue.

title: IUX-MANUAL-001 — Nothing has ever been validated on a real device
body:
The manual validation register is **empty**. In forty-two missions, nobody has run TalkBack, Voice Access or a D-pad on real hardware.

Everything this repository asserts about accessibility is measured on a semantics tree in a unit test. That is a great deal — 1976 tests, every claim probed rather than read — and it is **not the same thing** as a screen reader speaking.

## What a unit test cannot tell you

- **What TalkBack actually says.** The tree carries `label`, `hint`, `checked`, `expanded` and a role. What gets spoken, in what order, and whether an unselected state is voiced at all, is the platform's decision. `docs/components/bottom-navigation.md` already says so explicitly and declines to claim otherwise.
- **Whether a live region is announced.** Every pattern that uses one documents it as *a request, not a guarantee*.
- **Whether announcement timing collides.** IUX-033 refused a progress bar because it would put a second utterance in the same frame as a focus move — argued, never heard.
- **Voice Access.** Whether every control can be addressed by its visible name.
- **A physical D-pad.** Traversal order, and whether any surface is a trap.

## Why this is a release blocker

For a framework whose entire proposition is that accessibility is the design constraint rather than a checklist, shipping without one hardware session is the hardest gap to defend. It is also the only blocker that needs a **device** rather than a decision.

## Suggested scope for a first session

Both demo applications install on Android today (`apps/catalog`, `apps/pilot`). The catalog carries three stress axes and a "worst case" preset; the pilot is a real four-screen flow. A first pass over: bottom navigation, a form refusal, an empty state, a destructive flow with undo, and a permission rationale — at 100% and 200% text, with TalkBack on.

Findings belong in `docs/evidence/semantic-tokens-and-accessibility.md`, which is where every other measurement in this project lives.

> Talkback gestures that you will likely use are:  
> 1. Double Tap with one finger to simulate tapping on an icon.  
> 2. Flick or swipe with one finger to move forward or backward through the screen’s contents.

title: Android: Enabled services
body:
## Description
Similar to issue #30864 and heavily intertwined with #30863, it is sometimes useful to query what accessibility services a user has currently enabled. This would allow your to tailor your app's UI to the specific service. For example, if a user has the "Talkback" screen reader service enabled, you probably don't want videos to auto-play, as the audio would be interruptive to the screen readers announcements, and if auto-played without audio the videos would be playing and taking bandwidth without the user likely  realizing this was happening.

Right now, there *is* a method in the AccessibilityInfo API to detect talkback specifically (isScreenReaderEnabled), but there is not a general purpose method to get a list of all enabled services.

## React Native version:
v0.63

## Expected Behavior
The AccessibilityInfo API should have some general purpose method to get a list of all enabled services.

## Android Details
This functionality is available in the AccessibilityManager class via the getEnabledAccessibilityServiceList method.
https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/accessibility/AccessibilityManager#getEnabledAccessibilityServiceList(int)

title: Enable keyboard-first workspace navigation
Table: keyboard navigation between rows (APG grid/treegrid)
body:
## Problem

Nothing lets a keyboard user move between rows or cells. ADR-0029
(directives own accessibility, 2026-10-01) makes this the library's
job: category 5, keyboard navigation. No feature owns it today.

Raised by expansion OQ-exp-9 (step to the next/previous row while a
detail is open). The consumer has to search `renderRows()` and handle
the edge cases themselves.

## Scope

A cross-feature keyboard-navigation capability, owned by the core
table/row directives, following the APG grid/treegrid patterns:

- **One Tab stop** into the table; arrow keys move within it.
- **Row stepping:** ↑/↓ go to the next/previous visible data row.
  Group headers are rows you can step to (or are skipped where the
  feature says so), and stepping stops at the end with no wrap. The
  rule reads `renderRows()` order, so it's the same for every feature.
- **Home/End** (and cell navigation, if the grid pattern needs it).
- **Ignore keys from editable targets** (input, textarea, select,
  contenteditable).
- **Focus is never lost** when the focused row is removed, filtered out
  or re-sorted (ADR-0029 category 6).

Features plug in:
- **Expansion panel:** in single-open mode, the open panel follows the
  focused row, which is how a side panel steps with ↓ (story 1.6).
- **Tree:** →/← expand/collapse (treegrid).
- **Grouping:** group headers are steppable rows.

## Decide in the spec

- grid vs treegrid roles once tree/grouping are composed
- row-only vs cell-level navigation
- whether a group header counts as a step
- how a side panel outside the table receives the step (no DOM listener
  in consumer layout)

## Not blocking

#190. Story D (side panel) adds ↑/↓ once this ships.

## Context

- `libs/table/docs/adr/0029-directives-own-accessibility.md`, category 5
- `libs/table/docs/3-ui/cross-cutting/accessibility.md`
- `libs/table/docs/0-product/expansion.md`: OQ-exp-9, story 1.6
- `libs/table/docs/decisions/expansion.md`: E43
- APG grid: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/
- APG treegrid: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/treegrid/

## Pipeline

```yaml
workspace: null
grill: none
spec: none
tasks: none
readiness: needs:grill
assessed: 2026-10-01 - cross-feature capability with open design
  questions (grid vs treegrid, cell vs row, group headers, out-of-table
  panels); needs a grill before a spec.
```

title: Add keyboard navigation to cast scroll section
body:
## Description
The cast scroll section on the Detail page could benefit from keyboard accessibility. Users should be able to navigate between cast members using arrow keys when the section is focused.

## Proposed Solution

title: Make the desktop workflow keyboard-accessible and high-DPI robust
body:
## Problem

The Tk desktop view has some focus support, Return bindings, and a wide/stacked layout, but there is no documented keyboard interaction model or verification for focus order, visible focus, assistive-technology names, contrast, or Windows high-DPI scaling. A visually usable window can still be difficult or impossible to operate with a keyboard, screen reader, or enlarged display settings.

## Desired outcome

Make every primary BelegDock workflow reachable without a mouse, predictable when using keyboard navigation, and usable at the supported Windows and Linux display-scaling settings. Status and error meaning must not depend on color alone.

## Scope and exclusions

### In scope

- Define and implement a keyboard model for label selection, candidate multi-selection, staging, document selection, detail copying, upload confirmation, cancellation, and recovery guidance.
- Ensure logical focus order, visible focus indicators, useful control labels, and non-mouse access to all actions.
- Verify text scaling and the existing wide/stacked layouts at representative Windows scaling levels and Linux desktop settings.
- Check contrast, status communication, and dialogs for accessibility regressions.
- Add synthetic Tk tests for focus, bindings, and layout geometry plus a native Windows accessibility/manual smoke check.
- Record any limitations imposed by Tkinter and the evidence needed for the separate UI-toolkit evaluation.

### Out of scope

- Changing the Gmail, Lexware, staging, upload, or recovery state machine.
- A general internationalization framework or a new language.
- A claim of formal certification or complete screen-reader support without a defined target and test matrix.
- Replacing Tkinter as part of this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- A keyboard-only user can complete label selection, candidate selection, staging, document inspection, and the single-document upload confirmation without a mouse.
- Focus order is logical, focus is always visible, and no action is reachable only through pointer input.
- Controls and status/error states have understandable names and do not communicate state through color alone.
- At 100%, 125%, 150%, and 200% Windows scaling, and representative Linux scaling, the wide and narrow layouts remain usable with no clipped controls or unreachable actions.
- Focus, keyboard, and layout tests pass offline, and a native Windows check records the tested scaling and keyboard path.
- Any Tkinter limitation is documented with a reproducible case and linked to the toolkit decision rather than hidden behind a test-only workaround.

## Open questions

- Which accessibility standard or checklist should be the target for the pilot?
- Which Windows and Linux screen readers and scaling settings are supported for the first release?
- Are there existing brand colors that must be preserved, or may the palette be adjusted for contrast?
- If Tkinter cannot provide the required semantics, what evidence is sufficient to justify a toolkit change?
